Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

would verb

if …: I would go if I could

also ’d (would), would have, wouldn’t, if I were you, would (in reported speech)

classical

Publil. Sent. Q 83: Quis miserum scīret, verba nisi habēret dolor?

facerem, sī possem

the imperfect subjunctive in both clauses: unreal in the present

I would do it if I could (but I can’t)

For what is not so now. The two clauses may differ in time: quō tē modō accēpissem, nisi īrātus essem!, how I would have treated you, if I were not angry (Cic. Tusc. 4.78).

Other words

  • fēcissem, sī potuissem — I would have done it if I had been able

    the pluperfect subjunctive in both clauses: unreal in the past · also used · classical · Cic. Sen. 11: nisi tū āmīsissēs, numquam recēpissem

  • faciam, sī possim — I would (should) do it if I could (imagined)

    the present subjunctive in both clauses: a supposition · also used · classical · Publil. Sent. N 2: Nīl peccent oculī, sī animus oculīs imperet.; Plaut. Stich. 486b: Sī possim, velim.

    For what may yet be, only supposed. So the polite velim, “I’d like” (see want).

  • futūrum esse (the future infinitive) — would, in reported speech: he said he would …

    the future infinitive in an accusative and infinitive · also used · classical · Liv. 2.10.4: sē impetum hostium … exceptūrum

    After a verb of saying or thinking, English “would” of the future is the future infinitive, its participle agreeing with the subject; esse is often left out.

Examples

  • Quis miserum scīret, verba nisi habēret dolor?

    Who would know a man was unhappy, if pain had no words?Publil. Sent. Q 83

  • quō tē modō, inquit, accēpissem, nisi īrātus essem!

    “How I would have treated you,” he said, “if I weren’t angry!”Cic. Tusc. 4.78

  • 'certē,' inquit rīdēns, 'nam nisi tū āmīsissēs, numquam recēpissem'

    “Certainly,” he said, laughing, “for if you hadn’t lost it, I would never have taken it back.”Cic. Sen. 11

  • Nīl peccent oculī, sī animus oculīs imperet.

    The eyes would do no wrong, if the mind ruled them.Publil. Sent. N 2

  • sī mihi Nausicaa patriōs concēderet hortōs, Alcinoō possem dīcere "mālō meōs"

    if Nausicaa offered me her father’s gardens, I could say to Alcinous, “I prefer my own”Mart. 12.31.9–10

  • sē impetum hostium, quantum corpore ūnō posset obsistī, exceptūrum

    (he said) that he would take the enemy’s charge himself, as far as one body could hold itLiv. 2.10.4

See also if, want, used to, rather, able.
